CLIPPER SHIP "OCEAN EXPRESS"
The front cover of this menu is a reproduction of an authentic Currier & Ives clipper ship print.
Currier & Ives, known as the "Printmakers of America", graphically preserved the glorious clipper
ship era in a magnificent series of clipper ship prints. This print, one of a series, is being reproduced
through the courtesy of The Mariners Museum, Newport News, Virginia.
America, as a nation and a people, practically sprang from the sea. In the years 1850 to 1875,
the swift and graceful clipper ships were the dominant masters of the sea. They brought unprece-
dented growth and prosperity to the United States. The clipper ship "Ocean Express" was built by
D. O. Curtis in Medford, Massachusetts in 1855. She was employed in the lucrative tea and opium
trade from China and the frenzied, record-breaking voyages around Cape Horn. Under favorable
winds this ship was capable of the remarkable feat of 330 miles a day. Speed from the very earliest
days had been bound inextricably with trade, and now it became a topic of great interest, much
excitement and many wagers.
The decline of the "Ocean Express" is attributed to the collapse of the gold boom in California,
the extensive use of steamships and the disruptive effects of the Civil War. Discovery and exploita-
tion of the West succeeded in luring American men from the sea of their heritage, inland to a new
way of life.
Like Pan Am's modern Clippers* of the air, the early clipper ships traveled the lanes of com-
merce to all the far places of the world ... to Japan ... to Australia... and, in the days of the
great gold rusn, Irom America's east coast, around Cape horn,
South America, to California.
Our current equipment... the Clipper fleet of the Twentieth Century... consists of the finest
commercial aircraft ever developed —aircraft that have helped us establish an unparalleled record
for safety, speed and service.
